standard.title: Locate and Identify Primary and Secondary Sources
standard.description: locate and identify primary and secondary sources to use in historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: In Year 7 students located and identified primary and secondary sources (AC9HH7S02). In Year 8 they continued this practice (AC9HH8S02). Y9 extends the scope to include a wider range of repositories — archives, museums, online collections — and introduces digital data sources and the role of technology in enabling access to historical sources.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate and identify primary and secondary sources from a range of repositories, including digital collections, to use in historical inquiry.

nodes.label: Locating sources across repositories
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate historical sources from archives, museums and online collections, and explain how technology has enabled access to sources previously available only to specialist researchers.
nodes.minimum_width: Locate at least one primary source and one secondary source from different repositories (e.g. an online archive and a published work), identifying where each was found.
nodes.typical_width: Locate historical sources from archives, museums and online collections (e.g. National Archives of Australia, Trove, Australian War Memorial, state library digitised collections); recognise how technology enables access to sources that historians use; compare sources across repositories to understand what different collections offer and what they omit.
wider: Locate sources across multiple repositories for the same historical topic and compare what each repository offers, what is digitised, and what remains accessible only in physical form — developing awareness of how source availability shapes historical inquiry

Use digital historical databases (e.g. Trove, National Archives of Australia) to investigate how digitisation has changed access to historical sources — reflecting on what this means for who can do history
Locate sources in both English and translated form where available (e.g. sources from Asian societies being studied) and reflect on how translation and access intersect

response_modes.reason: Using multiple repositories (physical archives, museum collections, digitised databases) develops genuine source literacy — students who only use Google searches have a narrow understanding of how historical evidence is organised and accessed.

success_criteria: Locates at least two sources from different types of repository (e.g. a digitised archive and a published secondary source)
Identifies the repository and explains why it was a useful place to search for sources on the inquiry topic

nodes.label: Comparing sources and using digital data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare sources across repositories to analyse changes over time, including using digital data sources such as immigration records.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two sources on the same topic and identify at least one difference in what they offer as evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Compare sources to analyse changes over time including data from online records such as immigration records; explain how quantitative data sources (immigration records, census data, ship manifests) differ from qualitative primary sources in what they reveal and conceal; locate and compare multiple sources on the same inquiry question to assess convergence and divergence in what sources show.
wider: Use quantitative digital sources (e.g. immigration records, population census data from the period) alongside qualitative primary sources (diaries, newspapers) for the same inquiry question — practising the integration of different source types

Investigate a specific historical question using only digitised sources from one major repository, then assess what the inquiry is missing compared to a broader source search — developing critical awareness of how source selection shapes historical conclusions

response_modes.reason: Using both quantitative digital sources and qualitative primary sources for the same inquiry question is a distinct task context — practising both develops a more complete repertoire of source-locating skill.

success_criteria: Compares at least two sources and identifies at least one difference in what they offer as historical evidence
Explains how at least one digital or data source differs from a qualitative primary source in what it reveals about the past
